Future work should include more detailed behavioral studies, pilot programs, and surveys to better understand the drivers and barriers to tariff and technology adoption, as well as customer engagement with dynamic pricing features. Only by accounting for these behavioral nuances can the true impact of dynamic electricity pricing be accurately forecasted. 5 Conclusion This study provides valuable insights into the potential for electricity load flexibility in response to hourly dynamic pricing. Through the development of load response models and analysis of behind-the-meter technologies like batteries, the study highlights the opportunities for customers to shift their energy usage in response to price signals. We find that the subset of end use loads modeled in the study have the potential to substantially reshape the system load, reducing peak demands, lowering overall emissions, and creating a more renewable-friendly net load shape. Further, based on expected 2030 system load profiles and dynamic tariff designs explored here, enabling end use loads to respond to dynamic prices will be broadly cost effective across end uses and customer groups. The three tariff design scenarios studied here (Full, Medium, and Mild) produce similar technical potential impacts in terms of the induced load response but vary greatly in the value they offer to customers. Particularly on the Mild tariff, commercial cooling customers’ economic potential is significantly lowered, and the revenue opportunity for behind- the-meter batteries is negligible. However, the results are contingent on several assumptions, including 100% adoption of dynamic tariffs and enabling technologies, and do not fully account for the complexities of real-world behaviors, tariff designs, or more recent evolutions in electricity demand patterns.
